n: Back in Jerusalem, Rehoboam musters 180,000 soldiers from Judah and Benjamin to win back the northern tribes by force.

f.g: The two tribes that stayed loyal to David’s house (along with most priests and Levites).

n: God speaks to a prophet named Shemaiah.
Shemaiah is to deliver God’s message to the king and all the people of Judah and Benjamin.
God forbids civil war: do not fight your own brothers, because this division is My doing. Remarkably, Rehoboam and his army listen and go home.

f.g: The northern tribes were still kin — fellow descendants of Jacob.

f.w: this thing is done of me

n: Instead of attacking the north, Rehoboam strengthens Judah’s defenses by fortifying towns.
The list of fortified towns begins with Bethlehem (David’s hometown), Etam, and Tekoa (later the home of the prophet Amos) — all south of Jerusalem.
More towns: Beth-zur, Socoh, and Adullam — forts in the hills and western foothills. Adullam was where David once hid in a cave.
Gath (once a Philistine city), Mareshah, and Ziph complete the southwestern line of defense.

f.g: Goliath’s hometown, at this time apparently under Judah’s control.

n: Adoraim, Lachish, and Azekah guarded the southwest approaches. Lachish became one of Judah’s most important fortresses.
Zorah, Aijalon, and Hebron complete the list. Most of these forts faced west and south, suggesting Rehoboam feared Egypt and the coastlands more than Israel.
He strengthened the fortresses, posted commanders, and stocked them with food, oil, and wine to withstand sieges.
Each city was armed with shields and spears and made very strong, keeping Judah and Benjamin secure.
Priests and Levites from all over the north came to support Rehoboam. True worshippers gathered where true worship continued.
The Levites left their homes and lands in the north because Jeroboam had barred them from serving as priests of the Lord. They chose faith over property.

f.g: Pasture lands around the Levitical towns.

n: Jeroboam appointed his own priests for the hill shrines, for goat-idols, and for the golden calves he had made at Bethel and Dan.

f.g: Hebrew se‘irim — goat-demons or goat idols.

f.w: the calves which he had made

n: Faithful people from every tribe who set their hearts to seek the Lord also came to Jerusalem to worship. The southern kingdom thus kept members of all twelve tribes.

f.w: set their hearts to seek the LORD

n: These faithful newcomers strengthened Judah for three years, while the kingdom followed the ways of David and Solomon. Faithfulness is the real strength of a nation.
Rehoboam married Mahalath, a granddaughter of David, and Abihail, a descendant of David’s brother Eliab. These marriages kept power within the royal family.
Mahalath bore him three sons: Jeush, Shamariah, and Zaham.
He also married Maachah, a descendant (probably granddaughter) of David’s rebellious son Absalom. Her son Abijah would become the next king.
Rehoboam loved Maachah most among his eighteen wives and sixty concubines, and had eighty-eight children. Kings were forbidden to multiply wives, but royal custom often ignored that.
He made Maachah’s son Abijah chief prince among his brothers, intending him to be king.
Shrewdly, Rehoboam spread his sons out among the fortified cities, giving them provisions and wives. This kept them busy and loyal and avoided rivalry at the capital.

f.g: Or ‘he sought many wives for them’ — for his sons.
